Abstract: Interpretable machine learning (ML) paired with clinical decision support systems (CDSS) is revolutionizing healthcare in the context of enhancing transparency, personalization, and trust. This survey of 25 recent articles demonstrates that explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is essential to enhance clinician adoption and patient outcomes in different clinical settings, such as oncology, emergency medicine, and mental health. Scholars note that to make AI human-centric, promote cooperation between clinicians and algorithms, and provide the transparency of data, researchers need to design AI in a more human-centric manner, which will help to align the use of ML tools with ethical, fair, and realistic principles. Although these have been made, there are still difficulties in the field, including the need to balance model accuracy and interpretability, deal with biases, and incorporate them into current clinical practice. New approaches are being designed, such as the use of electronic health records, engaging end-users in the development of designs, and the use of new approaches of explanations, such as data-centric and proximity-informed explanations.

Abstract: In medicine, triage is a process that rations health services towards patients who are most in need of immediate care. Abstract: Ectopic pregnancy (EP) is a significant cause of maternal morbidity and mortality, particularly in the first trimester. It occurs when a fertilized ovum implants outside the uterine cavity, with the fallopian tubes being the most common location. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical to prevent complications such as tubal rupture and hemorrhage. Traditional diagnostic methods rely on transvaginal ultrasound (TVUSG) and serial  $\beta $ -hCG measurements, but these approaches can sometimes yield inconclusive results. Recent progress in artificial intelligence has demonstrated potential for improving the precision of ectopic pregnancy detection. This study examines the use of artificial intelligence-based classification models to predict pregnancy outcomes using routinely available clinical data. The dataset comprises 310 patient records collected from real-world clinical practice. Several classification approaches were evaluated, with particular emphasis on tree-based ensemble models. Experimental results indicate that the LightGBM DART model outperformed the other evaluated classifiers, achieving the highest overall performance with an accuracy of 0.9161, a macro-AUC of 0.9409, and a balanced accuracy of 0.9080, followed by CatBoost and Histogram-based Gradient Boosting models. These findings suggest that explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-based predictive models may support early and accurate diagnosis during the early follow-up period (Day 0–12), assist clinicians in timely decision-making, and potentially improve patient management, rather than serving as a standalone tool for initial Day-0 triage.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered e-triage systems are transforming patient intake and clinical decision-making by automating workflows and improving diagnostic precision. Abstract: Triage in emergency departments (EDs) is fundamental in prioritizing patient care and optimizing the allocation of limited healthcare resources. However, conventional triage systems remain susceptible to inconsistencies such as undertriage and overtriage, particularly in high-demand clinical environments. This study presents a machine learning-based approach for predicting triage levels using structured data from the emergency unit of a high-complexity regional hospital in Chile. The dataset was filtered to include only adult and dental consultation records, excluding pediatric and obstetric-gynecological cases due to their different clinical characteristics. Patients were categorized into five triage levels (C1 to C5), revealing a strong class imbalance, with C2 and C3 comprising nearly 90% of all records. The study implemented three tree-based gradient boosting algorithms, XGBoost, CatBoost, and LightGBM, in conjunction with Bayesian hyperparameter optimization and SVMSMOTE to mitigate class imbalance. Data preprocessing involved Random Forest-based imputation, standardization of numerical features, and one-hot encoding of categorical variables. The results indicate that XGBoost outperformed CatBoost and LightGBM in terms of overall accuracy (0.73) and weighted F1-score (0.72), particularly in the most frequent categories (C2 and C3). CatBoost, while exhibiting slightly lower global accuracy, demonstrated greater sensitivity in the minority class C1. However, all three models showed limitations in predicting the C5 category. The main contribution of this work is to demonstrate the feasibility and limitations of multiclass (C1–C5) triage prediction using gradient boosting models with Bayesian optimization and SHAP interpretability under extreme class imbalance.

Abstract: This study explores the application of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in the context of medical image analysis within medical cyber-physical systems (MCPS) to enhance transparency and trustworthiness. Meanwhile, this study proposes an explainable framework that integrates machine learning and knowledge reasoning. The explainability of the model is realized when the framework evolution target feature results and reasoning results are the same and are relatively reliable. However, using these technologies also presents new challenges, including the need to ensure the security and privacy of patient data from Internet of Medical Things (IoMT). Therefore, attack detection is an essential aspect of MCPS security. For the MCPS model with only sensor attacks, the necessary and sufficient conditions for detecting attacks are given based on the definition of sparse observability. The corresponding attack detector and state estimator are designed by assuming that some IoMT sensors are under protection. It is expounded that the IoMT sensors under protection play an important role in improving the efficiency of attack detection and state estimation. The experimental results show that the XAI in the context of medical image analysis within MCPS improves the accuracy of lesion classification, effectively removes low-quality medical images, and realizes the explainability of recognition results. This helps doctors understand the logic of the system's decision-making and can choose whether to trust the results based on the explanation given by the framework.

Abstract: The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) has transformed traditional healthcare systems by enabling real-time monitoring, remote diagnostics, and data-driven treatment. However, security and privacy remain significant concerns for IoMT adoption due to the sensitive nature of medical data. Therefore, we propose an integrated framework leveraging blockchain and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to enable secure, intelligent, and transparent management of IoMT data. First, the traceability and tamper-proof of blockchain are used to realize the secure transaction of IoMT data, transforming the secure transaction of IoMT data into a two-stage Stackelberg game. The dual-chain architecture is used to ensure the security and privacy protection of the transaction. The main-chain manages regular IoMT data transactions, while the side-chain deals with data trading activities aimed at resale. Simultaneously, the perceptual hash technology is used to realize data rights confirmation, which maximally protects the rights and interests of each participant in the transaction. Subsequently, medical time-series data is modeled using bidirectional simple recurrent units to detect anomalies and cyberthreats accurately while overcoming vanishing gradients. Lastly, an adversarial sample generation method based on local interpretable model-agnostic explanations is provided to evaluate, secure, and improve the anomaly detection model, as well as to make it more explainable and resilient to possible adversarial attacks. Simulation results are provided to illustrate the high performance of the integrated secure data management framework leveraging blockchain and XAI, compared with the benchmarks.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in text classification, but their complexity hinders interpretability, making it difficult to understand the reasoning behind their predictions. Explainable AI (XAI) methods like LIME and SHAP offer local explanations by identifying influential words, but they rely on computationally expensive perturbations. These methods typically generate thousands of perturbed sentences and perform inferences on each, incurring a substantial computational burden, especially with LLMs. To address this, we propose Perturbation-free Local Explanation (PLEX), a novel method that leverages the contextual embeddings extracted from the LLM and a “Siamese network” style neural network trained to align with feature importance scores. This one-off training eliminates the need for subsequent perturbations, enabling efficient explanations for any new sentence. We demonstrate PLEX's effectiveness on four different classification tasks (sentiment, fake news, fake COVID-19 news and depression), showing more than 92% agreement with LIME and SHAP. Our evaluation using a “stress test” reveals that PLEX accurately identifies influential words, leading to a similar decline in classification accuracy as observed with LIME and SHAP when these words are removed. Notably, in some cases, PLEX demonstrates superior performance in capturing the impact of key features. PLEX dramatically accelerates explanation, reducing time and computational overhead by two and four orders of magnitude, respectively. This work offers a promising solution for explainable LLM-based text classification.

Abstract: Early and accurate triage of traumatic brain injury is critical for guiding treatment decisions that optimize patient outcomes. A major early clinical decision point occurs in the emergency department, where providers must decide whether to admit or discharge patients with head injuries, yet these decisions are often inconsistent and rarely supported by case-based frameworks. Here, we introduce RAPID-TBI (Retrieval Augmented Prediction for Informed Disposition in Traumatic Brain Injury), a multimodal system that predicts emergency department disposition using example-based retrieval to emulate clinical case-based reasoning. RAPID-TBI achieves state-of-the-art classification performance while enhancing interpretability by retrieving similar patients to inform predictions. Using a large multimodal TBI dataset from a major U.S. hospital system, RAPID-TBI integrates head CT scans, radiology reports, exam findings, laboratory values, vitals, and demographics through an attention-based encoder that generates patient embeddings for disposition classification. We further assessed RAPID-TBI across institutional and temporal generalizability, showing consistent performance and resilience to shifts in data distribution. Finally, we explored small language models as prompt-based classifiers for retrieval-guided prediction without fine-tuning. Together, these components enable RAPID-TBI to deliver consistent, individualized, and clinically grounded predictions, a promising step toward trustworthy, personalized decision support in TBI care.

Abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is one of the leading causes of global mortality and disability. Early identification and risk prediction of CVD are crucial for its prevention and effective clinical management. This study proposes a CVD risk prediction model based on the Fast-Tunable Optimized Stacked Ensemble Learning (FT-OSEL) architecture. Building upon the original Optimized Stacked Ensemble Learning (OSEL) framework, FT-OSEL integrates lightweight network structures, adaptive fine-tuning mechanisms, parallel training strategies leveraging task-level parallelism, and knowledge distillation techniques, achieving significant improvements in training speed, prediction accuracy, and fine-tunability. The proposed model enables interpretable risk factor analysis and probabilistic predictions through temperature-scaled knowledge distillation, where the original OSEL serves as the teacher model and FT-OSEL as the student model. It further integrates established interpretability techniques—SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME)—to enhance transparency. Cross-dataset validation on an independent external cohort confirms its generalization capability. Experimental results indicate that FT-OSEL not only surpasses conventional approaches but also improves upon the original OSEL architecture, offering a more efficient and interpretable solution for early CVD screening.

Abstract: It is critically important to have dependable tools available to help identify inpatients during admission for those patients at highest risk for in-hospital death due to COVID19. Abstract: Between January and October of 2020, the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) virus has infected more than 34 million persons in a worldwide pandemic leading to over one million deaths worldwide (data from the Johns Hopkins University). Abstract: Effective triage of aortic abnormalities on non-contrast CT (NCCT) is critical for emergency care. Yet automated detection remains difficult due to low vessel–background contrast, resulting in unstable pseudo-segmentations and unreliable supervision. It integrates three key modules: (1) Prompt-invariant Structural Embedding (PISE) enforces feature consistency across multiple SAM-based prompts; (2) Region-aware Disentanglement (RAD) isolates vessel-wall representations from surrounding tissues; (3) Consistency Evidence Map (CEM) provides transparent, radiologistaligned visualization of abnormal regions. This study establishes a structural self-supervised paradigm that converts foundation-model uncertainty into structure-aware supervision, advancing interpretable, label-efficient, and scalable medical imaging AI for clinical deployment.

Abstract: Pharmacovigilance has expanded rapidly with the growth of real-world data, yet traditional approaches still face major limitations, including severe under-reporting (¿90%), fragmented data sources, and delayed signal detection, despite rising data volumes such as FAERS exceeding 20 million reports. The literature describes applications from case intake and data cleaning through signal detection, causality assessment, and triage of safety issues, using information from spontaneous reporting systems, electronic health records, social media, and other large safety datasets. Across these settings, AI tools are used to structure free text safety narratives, extract adverse drug reactions, and support near real time monitoring and automated alerting, with reported adverse reaction extraction accuracies typically in the 82–95% range and F measures around 0.72–0.82. Several groups also report substantial gains in efficiency, such as shorter case processing times or reduced false positive signals, and some Bayesian and network-based models appear to shorten formal causality assessment and enable more proactive risk forecasting.
